strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: evaluating degrees of human contribution beyond binary AI-generated-text detection. It explicitly distinguishes informational contribution from human effort and acknowledges limitations concerning authorship and copyright.
The proposed likelihood-based score is simple, computationally practical, and explicitly formulated. It offers a useful starting point for studying how prompts influence generated content.

The experiments have substantial breadth: 2,000 source entries per domain across four domains, repeated generations, multiple models, and interventions on output length and temperature. The consistent ordering across generation modes supports the score’s usefulness as a coarse indicator of prompt influence.

Human pairwise judgments, 2,500 WildChat examples, and surrogate-model experiments extend evaluation beyond synthetic generation alone. Dataset links, model checkpoints, hardware information, and a code repository link support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central interpretation as a percentage of human-contributed information is insufficiently justified. Equation 5 computes a pointwise likelihood gain, which can be negative, as also visible in Figure 7. Moreover, the prompt-free probability p(y) is not demonstrated to be the marginal of the conditional generation process under a specified prompt distribution. The score may be useful, but its shared-information interpretation and precise attribution percentages require stronger probabilistic justification and calibration.

The text-only extension does not establish that it estimates the stated minimum contribution. Equations 6–9 provide a lower bound under a chosen plausibility constraint, without demonstrating tightness or coverage of actual generating prompts. Equation 10 equals 1 + log(τ)/(I(y)/N), a monotonic transformation of mean token surprisal. Consequently, ordinal trends cannot validate the thresholds 0.65 and 0.7 or the attribution scale. Additionally, the geometric-mean constraint does not prevent individual tokens from having extremely low probabilities, contrary to the accompanying explanation.

Most synthetic validation establishes expected ordering among polishing, summary, title, and subject prompts. These conditions also differ substantially in input length and copying opportunities. Without comparisons against input/output length ratios, lexical overlap, and likelihood or perplexity baselines, the experiments do not establish what the proposed normalization contributes. Controlled comparisons that separate retained input information from these surface cues would strengthen construct validity.

The reported 97.4% human agreement is conditional on selecting pairs whose proposed scores already differ by more than 0.1. This favors comparisons the metric considers easy and leaves performance on close or within-category cases unresolved. A representative evaluation sampled independently of the score, with blinded judgments, annotator agreement, and uncertainty estimates, is needed to substantiate general reliability.

The robustness and transfer conclusions exceed the evidence. Two fixed stylistic instructions are limited stress tests, rather than attacks optimized against the metric. Likewise, preserving category-level ordering across surrogate models does not demonstrate agreement on individual attribution values. Claims should be narrowed or supported with targeted attack evaluation and quantitative analysis of scorer dependence.

Reproducibility cannot be fully assessed from the supplied manuscript: the repeatedly cited supplement containing sampling procedures, prompt templates, and annotation instructions is absent. Likelihood-scoring conventions, including chat formatting and treatment of decoding temperature, also need explicit documentation. Together with the unresolved interpretation and validation issues, these gaps warrant revision before a Findings recommendation.
